subject: Biology
title: Forensic DNA
description: A quick win: understand Forensic DNA.

hook.text: In 1984, Alec Jeffreys realized that everyone's DNA has a unique pattern—a genetic fingerprint.

buildup.text: Police can match DNA from a crime scene to a suspect using just a tiny sample.

discovery.text: DNA profiling compares repeating sequences at specific locations to create a unique profile.

twist.text: Forensic DNA has also freed over 375 wrongly convicted people through the Innocence Project.

climax.text: Genetic genealogy now helps solve cold cases decades old by matching DNA to family trees.

punchline.text: DNA never forgets, even if witnesses do.

quiz.question: Who discovered the technique of genetic fingerprinting?

details.summary: Forensic DNA analysis identifies individuals from biological evidence left at crime scenes. Short tandem repeat profiling creates a unique genetic fingerprint from skin cells, blood, or hair. DNA evidence has both convicted the guilty and exonerated the wrongly imprisoned.
details.whyItMatters: Forensic DNA revolutionized criminal justice by providing near-certain identification from trace evidence. Over 375 people in the US alone have been exonerated by DNA evidence after wrongful conviction.
takeaways: STR profiling analyzes repeating DNA sequences unique to each individual
Modern techniques can generate profiles from just a few cells
DNA databases enable cold case resolution through familial searching

faq.question: How reliable is DNA evidence in criminal cases?
faq.answer: When properly collected and analyzed, DNA profiling has error rates of less than one in a billion for full profiles. However, contamination, mixed samples, and interpretation errors can occur. The science is sound, but laboratory practices matter greatly.

faq.question: What is familial DNA searching?
faq.answer: When crime scene DNA does not match anyone in the database, analysts search for partial matches that suggest a close relative. This has solved high-profile cold cases like the Golden State Killer but raises privacy concerns about implicating family members.
